item.title: 2nd-generation planet: Was this world born around a dead star? - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• Planets form in the disks of dust and gas around newborn stars. These are called 1st-generation planets. But there are 2nd-generation planets too. A 2nd-generation planet can form in the material cast off from dead white dwarf stars.
  • Astronomers might have found a 2nd-generation planet around the white dwarf HS 0209+0832. It is in archives from the Hubble Space Telescope.
  • A “cold case” mystery about the white dwarf might now be solved thanks to the discovery.

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

Astronomers detect possible 2nd-generation planet

Planets typically form from the huge disks of dust and gas around newborn stars. These are what scientists call 1st-generation planets. But our universe evolves. So it should also contain 2nd-generation planets. A 2nd-generation planet is one that formed in material cast off from a dead star.

Now, for the first time, astronomers have detected a possible 2nd-generation planet that formed around a white dwarf. That is, the dense core left over by a dying star. They detected this planet in the data archive of the Hubble Space Telescope.

The potential discovery might solve an old “cold case” mystery about this white dwarf, which is named HS 0209+0832. Scientists have known for some time that this white dwarf has an unusually high amount of the element niobium in its atmosphere. And they’ve wondered … why? This phoenix-like planet rising from the dead star’s ashes might be the answer.

The researchers published their peer-reviewed paper in Nature Astronomy on October 5, 2026.

1st chapter of a long tale

We tend to think that after a star dies — probably along with its planets — that that’s it. But it’s not necessarily the end of the story. Astronomer Jamie Williams is the lead author of the new study at the University of Warwick in the U.K. He said:

Rather than the white dwarf stage being a kind of epilogue to the story of a star and its planets, this research points to the systems we are familiar with only being the first chapter of a potentially much longer tale, with some new characters showing up. That’s a really exciting prospect to pursue.

He added:

The 2nd-generation planets are worlds that form out of the material a star casts off as it dies. They’re incredibly rare, and finding one around a white dwarf was completely unexpected. It’s a bit like finding a planet that has risen from the ashes of the very star it once orbited.

Unknown chemical signatures

Ever since Hubble first observed HS 0209+0832 in 1999, a mystery has shrouded the white dwarf. Hubble detected about 100 chemical signatures that couldn’t be identified.

At the time, they remained unknown. But now, the researchers have used an updated chemical database. They found that the element niobium could explain many of these detections. And there was a lot of it. Williams said:

What Hubble is showing us in this white dwarf system is something we haven’t seen before: a high abundance of the element niobium, the signature of which I was unfamiliar with when I first found it in the archival data.

Niobium points to a 2nd-generation planet

The amount of niobium is also a clue. It suggested the presence of a planet that formed after the original star had died and became a white dwarf: a 2nd-generation planet. Co-author Nicholas Stone, a theoretical astrophysicist at the University of Wisconsin – Madison, said:

Niobium and other elements heavier than iron are astronomically special because, unlike many common elements, they are not formed in the cores of stars by thermonuclear fusion. Instead, these heavy elements can only be synthesized in the exotic conditions that briefly emerge inside dying stars. The presence of niobium is a signpost of these ‘death’ throes, and the expulsion of the dying star’s innards into space.

This pattern of elements is a telltale sign of the ‘s-process,’ a nuclear reaction that builds heavy elements inside dying stars during their bloated red giant phase. It’s a chemical signature no ordinary, ‘1st-generation’ planet should carry, which told us that this new planet was something different.

This is the first time that scientists have detected niobium in the atmosphere of a white dwarf, as co-author Boris Gaensicke, also at the University of Warwick, noted:

When Jamie asked me about niobium in relation to this study I was truly gobsmacked, as that element had not been reported in any other white dwarf analyzed to date. Once we realized it was there, everything fell into place.

What kind of planet is it?

The researchers estimate the planet itself to be about the size of Jupiter, therefore a gas giant. But it is quickly losing its atmosphere. Why is that?

The researchers say it is because the white dwarf is still very hot and bombarding the planet with intense radiation. Not surprising, since the planet orbits only 3.7 million miles (6 million kilometers) from the white dwarf. That’s a lot closer than Mercury is from the sun, at 36 million miles (58 million kilometers).

In fact, the planet might have a comet-like tail of material. This material would then fall back onto the white dwarf. That’s why the niobium is in the atmosphere of the white dwarf. And notably, Mercury also has a tail, of sodium.

Even though the white dwarf planet is losing its atmosphere, it will likely survive for a long time yet, as Williams noted:

If the 2nd-generation planet is there, I think it is likely to survive. Eventually the white dwarf will cool and then maintain a consistent temperature, with the planet in its stable habitable zone for millions of years.

A companion star?

The researchers also think that the white dwarf might have had a companion star. Williams said:

Forming the protoplanetary disc in this situation is not easy and helps explain why these planets are so rare. A single, isolated star dies and sheds mass in a roughly symmetrical way. To form a disc of material necessary to birth a planet, HS 0209+0832 likely required a companion star that pulled the ejected material back into orbit, rather than letting it escape.

Data about the 2nd-generation planet from other missions

Two other missions also provided additional data that support the existence of the 2nd-generation planet. These are NASA’s now-retired FUSE (Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer) and NASA’s TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite).

FUSE corroborated the findings of large amounts of niobium in the white dwarf system. And TESS observed the system for four straight months. It detected periodic variations in brightness of the white dwarf. These variations are evidence for a planet that orbits at only 3.7 million miles (6 million kilometers) from the white dwarf.

The HS 0209+0832 system will provide valuable data about white dwarfs and any planets that still exist around them. As Gaensicke said:

I think this research is an important example of the fact that scientific discovery is not a straight path. It often needs that magical moment when people discuss big questions on their minds and realize that together they can find unexpected answers.

Bottom line: Astronomers might have found a new 2nd-generation planet orbiting a white dwarf star. It could also help answer a “cold case” mystery about the white dwarf.

Source: Discovery of a 2nd-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf

Via NASA

item.title: Space is getting crowded. Here’s the latest satellite report - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Earth orbit is getting more crowded, and the consequences could be serious. The European Space Agency’s 2026 Space Environment Report warns that debris collisions could trigger a runaway chain reaction, making some orbital regions unsafe or unusable. Space hazards expert Jonathan McDowell joins EarthSky to explain what the report reveals, how dangerous conditions in space have become, and what we can do about it. Watch in the player above.

Science news, the night sky and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter

Space is getting crowded. Let’s look at the numbers

In September 2026, ESA’s Space Debris Office published its annual Space Environment Report. And, as you might suspect, the news is that space — in particular low Earth orbit — is getting more crowded. Here’s a look at the basic numbers as of October 2026 from OrbitalRadar.com:

  • 31,000+ total tracked objects in low Earth orbit
  • 18,600+ payloads in orbit, working and nonworking
  • 15,800+ of those are working satellites
  • 10,000+ of the working satellites are Starlink

And, according to ESA, the only place those numbers are going to go is up. ESA, which based its report on data through 2025, outlined some of the biggest concerns:

  • The number and scale of commercial satellite constellations continue to increase each year.  
  • Not enough satellites leave heavily congested orbits at the end of their lives, creating a growing collision risk. The expected number of objects and collisions in low-Earth orbit are skyrocketing in a runaway effect. (Read more: The Kessler syndrome) 
  • More than three intact satellites or rocket bodies are reentering every day. Plus, 10 new payloads are launched daily. (Read more: 1 to 2 Starlink satellites are falling back to Earth each day)
  • In 2026, ESA added an on-ground casualty risk of reentries. While the risk is still very low, the chance is still increasing every year due to increased traffic.  

Let’s visualize the numbers

Here are some graphics from ESA to help us visualize the numbers of satellites in orbit and being added to orbit.

The pluses and minuses of reentry

Because there are now so many satellites in low Earth orbit, it’s important that they get removed from orbit when they’ve reached the end of their lives. And one of the positive findings of ESA’s 2026 report was that there are more controlled reentries now. That means companies and governments are conducting planned end-of-life disposal of their satellites.

But reentries have drawbacks. As they burn up in our atmosphere, they deposit heavy metals. There are many issues this deposit could lead to, include damaging the ozone layer, affecting the climate and altering the atmosphere’s natural chemistry.

And then, of course, there’s the new metric ESA introduced this year: the risk of casualties on the ground. While you are still much more likely to be injured or killed in a car or on a staircase, the risk of harm from satellite reentry has naturally gone up as the number of reentering satellites goes up. More controlled reentries would help to mitigate this risk.

Space is getting crowded: What are the real risks?

The biggest immediate concern, as we send more and more satellites into low Earth orbit, is that the rising population seems unstoppable. That is, until collisions cascade into more collisions and make the environment unusable.

This idea that satellites will collide and create debris that produces more collisions until we have a runaway cascading effect is called the Kessler syndrome.

As recently as October 5, 2026, LeoLabs detected a satellite breakup in a crowded low-Earth environment. LeoLabs spotted multiple objects near the inactive Meteor 2-7 satellite after it passed over a radar station in Western Australia. Followup observations from other radars confirmed that a debris-generating event occurred. The company called it a:

… worrying trend for space safety and security.

But ESA — along with other space organizations — is working on ways to reduce the risk. This will involve cleaning up orbits and working toward a zero debris solution.

Bottom line: ESA has put out an annual report documenting the state of low Earth orbit. The number of satellites in orbit is skyrocketing, along with the chance for collisions and on-ground casualties.

Via ESA

item.title: Planetary systems fall into 2 distinct families, astronomers say - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

Planetary systems fall into 2 distinct families

Astronomers from the International Space Science Institute said on October 13, 2026, that planetary systems appear to fall into one of two families depending on their home star. After studying 300 of the best-characterized planetary systems in the Milky Way galaxy, they found that less massive stars tend to form planetary systems that are smaller in mass and width but with more planets. On the other hand, more massive stars tend to form planetary systems that are more chaotic and wider with more massive, though fewer, planets.

The researchers published their study in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Astronomy on October 13, 2026.

The 2 types of families

The researchers said that a planetary system’s host star appears to determine how its planets form and evolve. The amount of material in the cloud of gas and dust that forms the star influences what type of planetary family results. Let’s take a closer look at the two family types.

The compact planetary system

The compact, lower-mass planetary systems tend to orbit stars that are as massive as or less massive than our sun. These stars also tend to have similar or lower amounts of heavy elements. The width of the planetary system is smaller and it has less massive planets, but they’re packed more tightly. But not everything about this family type is diminutive. It tends to have more planets than the more massive planetary system.

Scientists said the lower-mass systems have neighboring planets that are similar to each other, or what they call “peas in a pod.” These systems have less gravitational upheaval and more orderly systems. To sum up:

  • Host stars are as massive as or less massive than our sun, with similar or lower amounts of heavy elements
  • Planets are less massive and more similar to each other
  • Orbits are compact, close to the host star
  • Dynamic history is less violent and closer to our solar system

The wider planetary system

The wider planetary systems have stars that are more massive than our sun. These stars have a higher proportion of heavy elements. This results in planets that are more massive, though fewer in number. However, these larger worlds orbiting their stars can gravitationally interact, causing instabilities. So the planets that survive these interactions are more likely to have varied orbits. To sum up this family:

  • Host stars are more massive than our sun, with more heavy elements
  • Planets are fewer but more massive
  • Orbits are wider and more varied
  • Dynamic history is violent with possible collisions and ejections

So why are wider systems unstable?

The wider planetary systems are more violent and chaotic, with planetary collisions and ejections. These processes can leave planets in a variety of orbits. Danae Polychroni, of the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics, explained why:

The scenarios that best reproduce the dynamical properties of the family of wide and massive systems are those in which the systems are unstable from birth. The greater abundance of material from which planets form around their host stars causes them to be born too large, preventing the system from remaining stable.

Sorting planetary systems

Co-author Diego Turrini of the International Space Science Institute said:

The fundamental question we started from was: What determines the characteristics of planetary systems as we see them today? Are they established at birth or sculpted by evolution over time? The truth, in the end, turned out to lie somewhere in the middle. Our results show that there is a genetic link between planetary systems and their stars, and that, depending on the star around which they are born, this link also determines their fate.

Co-author Camilla Danielski of the University of Valencia said:

The main difficulty during the data analysis was determining whether the two families of planetary systems were real or just an illusion created by the technological limits of current observational techniques. At the end of the path, it became clear that selection effects acted as the tip of the iceberg, revealing the existence of much deeper structural diversities between these systems.

The astronomers hope that understanding which stars create which planetary systems will help in the search for planets that could be home to life.

Bottom line: Astronomers studying planetary systems in the Milky Way have found they can be sorted into two families. These families are largely determined by the host star.

Source: Two families of multi-planet systems with distinct architectures and stellar hosts

Via International Space Science Institute

item.title: What star in the northeast flashes colorfully? It’s Capella! - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
You deserve a daily dose of good news. For the latest in science and the night sky, subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter.

Capella is the colorful, twinkling star in the northeast

This evening, check out one of the flashiest stars in the sky. It’s the brightest star in the northeast this month. It’s so bright that every year in northern autumn, we get questions from people in the Northern Hemisphere who see a star twinkling with colorful flashes. It lies low in the northeastern sky in early evening as seen from mid-northern locations. That star is Capella.

The reason it’s so flashy is because it’s a bright star shining near the horizon. That means its light is coming to us through our thick atmosphere. The wavering air makes its point of light jump around, split into colors and appear to flash.

If you could travel to it in space, you’d find that Capella is really two golden stars, both with roughly the same surface temperature as our local star, the sun … but both larger and brighter.

Capella is in the constellation Auriga the Charioteer. Since antiquity, Capella’s nickname has been the Goat Star. You might pick it out just by gazing northeastward from a Northern Hemisphere latitude during the evening hours in October. Capella climbs upward throughout the night, and this month soars high overhead in the wee hours before dawn.

Why stars twinkle or flash

So, Capella is a golden point of light that flashes red, green and blue when it’s low in the sky. Why does it do that?

The reality is that every star in the sky undergoes the same process as Capella when it twinkles. That is, every star’s light must shine through Earth’s atmosphere before reaching our eyes. But not every star flashes as noticeably as Capella. The flashes happen because Capella is low in the sky in the evening at this time of the year. And, when you look at an object low in the sky, you’re looking through more atmosphere than when the same object is overhead.

The atmosphere splits or refracts the star’s light, just as a prism splits sunlight.

So that’s where Capella’s red, green and blue flashes are coming from — not from the star itself, but from the refraction of its light by our atmosphere. When you see Capella higher in the sky, you’ll find that these glints of color will disappear.

By the way, why are these flashes of color so especially noticeable with Capella? The reason is simply that it’s a very bright star. It’s the sixth brightest star in Earth’s sky, not including our sun.

Here are 2 other flashing stars of autumn

If the flashy star you’re seeing doesn’t seem to be Capella (wrong time, wrong location), here are a couple of other options. Arcturus is in the northwest at this time of year. Follow the curving handle of the Big Dipper toward the horizon, and if it hits the star you’re wondering about, then you’re looking at Arcturus in Boötes.

Another option is Sirius. If you’re waking before dawn this time of the year, you’ll find Sirius toward the south. Check out the maps below to see which star is twinkling at you.

Bottom line: If you’re in Earth’s Northern Hemisphere and see a bright star twinkling with red, green and blue flashes low in the northeast on October evenings, it’s probably Capella. See charts here!

Did you see a strange cloud on the East Coast?

On Tuesday morning, October 13, 2026, a SpaceX Falcon rocket launched from Florida, sending a Dragon spacecraft to the International Space Station. This was a resupply mission, launching just before dawn. As the spacecraft headed upward through Earth’s atmosphere, it left behind a trail of exhaust. That trail expanded and was high enough to be sunlit by the approaching dawn. Observers often describe this phenomenon as the jellyfish effect.

We can see the jellyfish effect for the same reason we can see satellites orbiting Earth before sunrise and after sunset. The sun’s rays are still reaching the highest portions of our atmosphere, lighting the objects there, whether that be a satellite or water vapor.

Observers could see the jellyfish phenomenon from up to 800 miles away.

Bottom line: Many people up before sunrise on Tuesday morning saw a strange cloud. It was the plume from a SpaceX rocket headed for the space station.

item.title: Tiny Gold Nanogaps Could Crack the Chirality Puzzle - Universe Today
item.description: Looking for biosignatures across the solar system requires looking for asymmetry. Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, are famously either “left-handed” (L) or “right-handed” (D). We know abiotic processes (i.e. those that create amino acids but don’t involve life) create a 50/50 mixture of the two types, which is called a racemic mixture. But life as we know it almost exclusively relies on left-handed amino acids to fold proteins and right-handed ones to construct nucleic acids. So if we find an imbalance in the types of amino acids we analyze from somewhere in the solar system, it's a good indication that life is behind that imbalance. Differentiating between the two “chiralities”, as they’re called, is possible, but typically requires advanced equipment and chemical disposables that make them burdensome for spaceflight applications. But a new paper in Nature Communications from researchers led by Takahito Ohshiro and Masateru Taniguchi of Osaka University offers an alternative - a solid-state quantum tunneling sensor that can read the chirality of a single amino acid molecule using basically just some gold wire.

item.title: NASA’s Perseverance rover on Mars sets off-world driving record - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
You deserve a daily dose of good news. For the latest in science and the night sky, subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter.

Congratulations, Perseverance rover!

As of October 11, 2026, NASA’s Perseverance rover has driven 28.10 miles (45.22 km) on Mars. That’s a new off-world driving record for total distance driven by any vehicle on the surface of another world. The previous record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) was held by NASA’s Opportunity rover. Perseverance reached that mark on the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission. NASA said;

It covered in five and a half years a distance that took Opportunity almost 15.

The six-wheeled geologist has in less than six years surpassed a mark set by the agency’s Opportunity rover, which explored the Red Planet for nearly 15 years.

The milestone came as Perseverance traveled toward an area called Idubi through the region off the western rim of Jezero Crater nicknamed Lac de Charmes. There, the rover is investigating what may be some of the oldest terrain ever explored in the solar system.

The rocks and terrain of Lac de Charmes are so ancient that their Earthly equivalents have long since been erased by erosion and plate tectonics. But Mars doesn’t have tectonic plates. And Idubi is where the science team hopes to find traces of ancient hydrothermal (heated water) systems.

Humans set goals, Perseverance self-drives

Much of the credit belongs to Perseverance’s self-driving capability, NASA said. Using an autonomous navigation system known as AutoNav, the rover images the terrain while rolling, builds a 3D map of hazards, and plots its course between waypoints selected by rover planners on Earth — a capability the team calls thinking while driving.

Perseverance can do all that at or near its top speed, covering as much as 1,351 feet (412 meters) in a single sol.

The six-wheeled scientist has driven more than 90% of its total distance using AutoNav to evaluate the terrain. That’s in contrast to about 5% for the first Martian AutoNav system on Opportunity and its twin, Spirit. Where NASA’s first Mars rover, Sojourner, assessed the path ahead using 20 measurement points, Perseverance processes 600,000 with every look.

Steven Lee, the project manager of the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, said:

It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine. The original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving. We’ve blown well past that, and with all mobility systems fully operational and favorable extended-ground-life test results, we expect Perseverance to keep adding to this record for many years to come.

NASA recently approved the mission’s first extension, which began in October and will carry Perseverance’s exploration of the crater rim through roughly the end of 2028.

3 decades of Mars rovers

Perseverance’s record caps nearly three decades of NASA rover operations on Mars, each mission driving farther and more capably than the last.

The microwave-oven-size Sojourner rover covered about 330 feet (100 meters) during its 83-sol mission in 1997. The golf-cart-size twins Spirit and Opportunity arrived in 2004 with 90-sol prime missions. Spirit logged 4.8 miles (7.7 km) before succumbing to the Martian winter in 2010. Opportunity kept rolling for 5,111 sols, completing the first extraterrestrial marathon in 2015 and setting the record Perseverance has now surpassed. The agency’s Curiosity rover, which landed in Gale Crater in 2012 and remains hard at work, has logged more than 23.65 miles (38.07 kilometers).

Mark Maimone, deputy team chief for robotic operations on Perseverance, said:

The rover that broke this record did so by making its own decisions about the path. Given the autonomy to just go, Perseverance is a better driver than the one that landed, and we’re not done,

Our newest software teaches Perseverance to steer less and roll more, and to check its own position against orbital maps mid-drive.

The next frontier is sunlight itself. Glare in the navigation cameras is why we park by mid-afternoon if we’re driving toward the sun, and if we can teach the rover to see past those artifacts, every rover that follows gets a longer working day.

Not just Mars, and why it matters

The extraterrestrial off-road driving record isn’t limited to Mars: Lunar driving records were broken earlier in the journey. Perseverance rolled past both the 22.2 miles (35.7 kilometers) covered by Apollo 17 astronauts Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt in 1972 and the 24.2 miles (39 kilometers) driven by the Soviet Union’s Lunokhod 2 rover in 1973.

Setting distance records is just a bonus. Stamina and longer drives are putting more geologic diversity within reach faster — more outcrops examined and more of the Red Planet’s history read from its rocks. That reach carried Perseverance from an ancient lakebed up a fossilized river system, where the rover found a potential biosignature at a rock called Cheyava Falls, and on to the crater rim, where an entirely different kind of ancient habitat — hydrothermal (heated water) — may await.

Perseverance has collected 29 rock and regolith samples. The samples span the crater floor, a delta fan formed by a long-gone river, and now the crater rim. In the latter region, it has been exploring impact-generated rocks some 4 billion years old. On Earth, that chapter of planetary history has been almost entirely erased.

After Lac de Charmes, the rover will continue along the crater rim and head south during the extended mission towards Rainbow Falls, a 328-foot-wide (100-meter-wide) block of ancient crust uplifted by the impact that created Jezero.

Bottom line: The Mars Perseverance rover has set a new distance record on Mars. It has driven 28.10 miles (45.22 km). Perseverance reached that mark on October 11, 2026, the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission.

item.title: Weirdest cloud on Mars formed via ‘exotic physics’ - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• Clouds are fairly common on Mars, despite the thin atmosphere. And some of them can be a bit more unusual than others.
  • The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC), extending from the volcano Arsia Mons, is one such cloud. It reappears every spring and summer, forming downwind from the volcano. But how and why?
  • ‘Exotic physics,’ not actually seen before, can explain the behavior of the weirdest cloud on Mars, a new study from France says.

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

The weirdest cloud on Mars

Mars’ atmosphere is extremely thin. But the red planet does have clouds. And some of them can be … well, unusual.

The weirdest cloud on Mars is a vast, elongated formation extending from an ancient volcano on Mars, called Arsia Mons. So scientists call this cloud the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC). It forms every spring and summer, downwind of the volcano. It grows and then fades away every day during this period. But why and how?

The cloud can stretch up to 920 miles (1,500 km) in length! The European Space Agency’s Mars Express orbiter first saw the cloud in 2018. And it has often observed it ever since. But despite years of observations, its extraordinary length and daily cycle have remained difficult to explain.

The researchers, from Sorbonne University in Paris, France, said on October 7, 2026, that new simulations suggest that “exotic physics” might be behind this weird cloud.

They published their peer-reviewed paper in Nature Geoscience on October 7, 2026.

‘Exotic physics’ needed to explain weirdest cloud on Mars

Previous simulations weren’t able to model how the cloud should form. But now, the new simulations do, and reveal something interesting. Lead author Jorge Hernández-Bernal at LMD/CNRS/Sorbonne University said:

To create the AMEC in our modeling, we found that we needed to include some exotic physics … physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before. Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped.

An unexpected process

Most clouds — on both Mars and Earth — form in cool, moist air. The water vapor condenses onto particles floating in the atmosphere, such as salt, pollen, soot or dust.

But for the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud, something is different. The icy particles or droplets don’t need a “seed” particle to form. Hernández-Bernal said:

For the AMEC, it seems that cloud formation takes place without needing any of this ‘stuff.’ Water vapor turns directly into icy cloud particles without any middle step. It’s akin to droplets of condensation appearing in the middle of a room, rather than on a window. We call this homogeneous nucleation, and we’ve never seen it before in a planetary atmosphere. It’s wholly unexpected.

Rare process never seen before

Until now, this process has been theoretical, never seen in any planetary atmosphere. But scientists thought that it could happen. Maybe in the upper atmospheres of Venus or Earth.

And now, for the first time, they’ve seen it in action, on Mars.

Scientists think it requires “exceptional circumstances” to occur. This would be in extreme relative humidity levels of over 100,000 times those that we experience on Earth. As Hernández-Bernal noted:

We’ve not seen these conditions on Mars before, but our finding now strongly suggests that the planet’s humidity can indeed reach these extreme levels.

And it’s not only the humidity, but the location. The towering volcano, plus thin atmosphere, create just the right conditions for this kind of cloud to form.

Winds flow past Arsia Mons, and the volcano triggers a powerful wave that lifts moist parcels of air several kilometers up into the air in just a few minutes. This causes the atmosphere to cool rapidly, with temperatures dropping by 30 degrees in just 10 minutes.

The relative humidity levels also spike. And the water vapor spontaneously freezes directly into cloud particles.

The new model isn’t a complete 100% match for the observations by Mars Express, but it is impressive nonetheless. Hernández-Bernal said that:

… the result is remarkable. We don’t have nearly as much information about Mars’ atmosphere as we do about Earth’s, so reproducing the AMEC to this degree is a big success for the model.

How Mars Express solved the mystery?

So how did Mars Express make these new findings about the cloud?

It used its three onboard cameras: the Visual Monitoring Camera, the High Resolution Stereo Camera and OMEGA.  These cameras are able to image large swaths of the Martian surface at high resolution. Another advantage the orbiter has is that it can observe during morning hours. Only ESA’s ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter can also do that.

Mars Express can also observe the cloud and track its changes over periods of only a few hours. According to Mars Express Project Scientist Colin Wilson:

Mars Express can also track how the cloud is changing on timescales of mere hours, which gives us an unrivaled view of short-lived phenomena on the planet. Overall, this finding is a true accomplishment for the mission and its scientists: Mars Express discovered the AMEC, has followed up and monitored it for years, and is now helping reveal the secrets of its formation.

Bottom line: A new study of the oddest cloud on Mars, which reappears every year at the Arsia Mons volcano, says that “exotic physics” is required to explain its behavior.

Source: Homogeneous ice nucleation from water vapor suggested by elongated clouds on Mars

item.title: Amazon wildfires hide another threat to the rainforest - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Wildfires in the Amazon have consequences that go far beyond the destruction of vegetation, scientists say. A new study has revealed that ozone produced during these events also harms trees that survive the flames, damaging their leaves and making it harder for them to absorb carbon dioxide (CO2).

Though it’s less visible than the direct damage caused by fire, this effect poses a very real threat. It represents an additional loss for the rainforest’s carbon balance and can become more severe during periods of intense drought.

Researchers from the University of Exeter, ETH Zurich and James Cook University published their peer-reviewed study in the journal Communications Earth & Environment on October 7, 2026.

Amazon wildfires and human responsibility

Almost all fires in the Amazon are started by people, mainly to clear land for agriculture and cattle ranching. However, these fires can get out of control and spread into surrounding areas of rainforest, destroying vast stretches of woodland.

Wildfires release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. And they also produce pollutants that contribute to the formation of what’s called tropospheric ozone. That’s ozone — a gas composed of three oxygen atoms — that occurs in the troposphere — the lowest layer of the atmosphere — which extends from the Earth’s surface upwards.

Ozone is also found in the stratosphere, which is the atmospheric layer above the troposphere. In the stratosphere, ozone helps protect us from much of the sun’s ultraviolet radiation. But tropospheric ozone is harmful to human health and vegetation. It damages the leaves of surviving trees and reduces their ability to absorb carbon dioxide. In this way, wildfires not only release carbon by burning forests, but also make it harder for the surviving rainforest to absorb some of that carbon.

The threat to surviving trees

Tropospheric ozone pollution damages tree leaves and reduces the efficiency of photosynthesis, the process through which trees absorb carbon dioxide. As a result, even areas that have not been directly burned can lose some of their ability to remove carbon from the atmosphere.

The researchers estimate that this reduction in carbon uptake is equivalent to around 24% of the carbon released directly by wildfires. Flossie Brown, the study’s lead author from ETH Zurich, explains that the consequences of wildfires go beyond the emissions produced by combustion:

Forest fires don’t just release CO2 when they burn. They also contribute to the rise in ground-level ozone, a pollutant that damages the leaves of surviving trees and reduces their ability to keep absorbing carbon afterwards. We found this hidden effect is equivalent to around a quarter of the carbon released by the fires themselves — a significant loss to the Amazon’s carbon budget that hasn’t previously been considered.

To investigate this phenomenon, the team analyzed observations covering the period from 1997 to 2024 and used a global vegetation model. This allowed them to examine the relationship between wildfires, ozone damage and the Amazon’s ability to absorb carbon dioxide. The results also showed that the impact is not constant. Instead, it can become more severe when climatic conditions are particularly harsh.

El Niño and droughts can worsen the impact

Although human activities play a major role in many Amazon wildfires, climatic conditions can intensify their effects. Severe droughts put vegetation under greater stress and can worsen the damage suffered by the rainforest.

One important factor is El Niño. That’s the warm phase of a natural climate phenomenon that alters weather patterns in different parts of the world. It is not caused by human activity, but global warming raises baseline temperatures and can intensify some of its effects.

Three of the most severe Amazon droughts in recent decades — in 1997–1998, 2015–2016 and 2023–2024 — coincided with El Niño events. During the 2023–2024 drought, ozone-related damage almost doubled compared with the average for the previous decade.

The researchers warn that a strong El Niño event could once again create conditions that are damaging to the rainforest. However, this climate phenomenon should not be confused with the cause of deforestation. It can intensify the damage, but logging and burning associated with human land use remain fundamental factors that can be directly addressed.

Protecting the Amazon requires a joined-up approach

The findings show that the impact of wildfires extends far beyond the carbon dioxide they release as forests burn. Ozone pollution also weakens surviving trees and reduces the Amazon’s ability to remove carbon from the atmosphere. When this effect coincides with extreme climatic conditions, the consequences for the rainforest can be even more severe.

Stephen Sitch, from the University of Exeter, highlights that reducing deforestation and forest degradation would not only cut direct wildfire emissions, but also protect the rainforest from this additional loss of carbon:

Reducing deforestation and forest degradation would cut direct fire emissions — but our study shows it would also protect the Amazon from this secondary, invisible source of carbon loss.

As Alexander Cheesman, from James Cook University, points out:

These impacts interact and need to be considered together.

So protecting the Amazon means not only preventing more trees from burning, but also preserving the ability of the surviving rainforest to continue absorbing carbon dioxide. This requires action to tackle deforestation while also taking the effects of air pollution and climate change into account. Ignoring these connections means overlooking part of the problem.

Love wildlife and the natural world? Get the latest animal stories — as well as space and night sky updates delivered to your inbox.

Bottom line: Amazon wildfires are weakening the rainforest’s ability to absorb carbon, as ozone pollution damages trees that survive the flames.

Source: Fire-derived ozone intensifies carbon loss in Amazon forests under extreme droughts

Via University of Exeter

item.title: Arizona’s Chiricahua poised to become 64th US National Park - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
A viewing platform at Massai Point in Chiricahua National Monument. Will it become the 64th national park in the U.S.? Image via Lucy Whitt. Used with permission.

You deserve a daily dose of good news. For the latest in science and the night sky, subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter.

Arizona’s Chiricahua poised to become 64th US National Park

A quiet national monument tucked into southeastern Arizona is poised to become North America’s newest national park. Chiricahua National Monument — which towers with rock formations and is home to animals such as the coatimundi — could soon become the 64th national park in the United States. Chiricahua National Park would join the three other national parks in Arizona: Petrified Forest, Saguaro and the Grand Canyon.

On September 30, 2026, the U.S. Congress passed legislation to redesignate the monument as a national park. Now the bill just awaits the U.S. president’s signature.

The legislation keeps the existing boundaries of the park. It also doesn’t change the federal ownership and management of the park. What it will do is draw many more visitors to the area, which can be both a benefit and a drawback, especially in this time of cuts to the National Park Service’s budget.

Chiricahua is a wonderland of rocks

Chiricahua, sitting in the Chiricahua Mountains, is famous for its bizarre collection of rock formations. The National Park Service describes the landscape as a collection of rhyolite pinnacles and balanced rocks. Ancient volcanic eruptions some 27 million years ago led to what we see today as a wonderland of rocks.

The eruptions layered ash and molten rock that compacted into what geologists call rhyolite tuff. Eventually water and wind erosion wore down the softer parts of the rock. What remains are the stacked pinnacles and hoodoos we see today.

An International Dark Sky Park

Chiricahua National Monument is already designated an International Dark Sky Park. These parks conserve the night sky and are excellent for stargazing. And Arizona’s desert environment is already well-known for its night skies. It’s the home of many astronomy observatories.

Chiricahua is open 24 hours a day. The National Park Service suggests stargazing from locations such as Massai Point and Echo Canyon Trailhead. And, of course, campgrounds are another great spot. Just throw your sleeping bag under the stars!

What lives in these lands?

Chiricahua is home to a wide variety of animal life. Just a few of the many animals you might see here include black bears, white-tailed deer, rattlesnakes and the tiger salamander. Plus, some 200 species of birds have been documented here.

But one of the big draws for animal watchers in the park are the coatimundi. These long-tailed members of the raccoon family are more common in South America, but you can also find them here in the Chiricahua Mountains. Because coati are active during daylight hours and social animals, you have a good chance to see them playing together in the park.

Concerns with national park status

There are some concerns with changing the national monument to a national park. About 70,400 visitors came to Chiricahua in 2025. And it probably isn’t prepared for the increase in visitation once it receives national park status.

There is only one campground in Chiricahua, with 26 sites. There is no lodge. More tourism will mean more pressure on roads, trails, wildlife habitat, water resources and park staff. But more tourism could also be a boon to surrounding communities. And more visitors means more people will realize the value of this land and wish to protect it.

As always, the designation of land to a national park can have both benefits and drawbacks.

Have you visited Chiricahua National Monument? Let us know in the comments.

Bottom line: Chiricahua National Monument in the southeastern corner of Arizona is poised to become the U.S.’s 64th national park.

item.title: Check out the Double Cluster in Perseus on October evenings - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Catch the wonder of the night sky. Subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter for the latest in science, stars, planets and more.

Double Cluster in Perseus

The Double Cluster in Perseus consists of two open star clusters near each other on the sky’s dome. Amateur astronomers know them as h Persei and chi Persei. The two clusters reside in the northern part of the constellation Perseus the Hero, quite close to the constellation Cassiopeia the Queen.

If you have a dark sky and find Cassiopeia – which is easy, because the constellation has a distinctive M or W shape – be sure to look for Perseus, too. Then just scan between the two constellations with your binoculars for two glittering groups of stars. The Double Cluster – a breathtaking pair of open clusters, each containing supergiant suns – will be there.

These two star clusters are located about 7,500 light-years away. It’s amazing that we can see these stars at all across this great span of space. Plus, we know they must be intrinsically bright stars, or we wouldn’t be able to see them. Each cluster contains a few hundred stars, and, indeed, these stars are young, hot supergiant suns. They are many thousands of times more luminous than our sun.

Astronomers tell us that the Double Cluster lies within the Perseus arm of the Milky Way galaxy. However, our solar system resides in the inner part of the Orion arm. Therefore, looking at the Double Cluster, we are looking through our local spiral arm and all the way to the next spiral arm outward from the galactic center.

How to find the Double Cluster in Perseus

To locate the Double Cluster, find the W or M shaped constellation Cassiopeia the Queen. If your sky is dark enough, you will be able to see the graceful pattern of Perseus the Hero nearby. Then scan between them with binoculars to find the Double Cluster.

Starting at mid-northern latitudes, the Double Cluster is circumpolar, so it’s above the horizon every night of the year at any hour of the night. If you are farther south (but still in the Northern Hemisphere), try looking for the Double Cluster on any clear autumn or winter night.

But remember, the Double Cluster is harder to see when it’s close to the horizon. If you can’t spot it between Cassiopeia and Perseus, wait until later at night. Or look later in the year, when it’s higher in the sky.

For general reference, the Double Cluster is high in the sky when the Big Dipper is low, and vice versa. Because the Big Dipper is lowest in the northern sky on late autumn and early winter evenings, the Double Cluster is highest in the northern sky at these times. As a matter of fact, the Double Cluster is pretty much always visible in the evening except in late spring and summer.

The Double Cluster in Perseus is visible to the unaided eye

The Double Cluster rates among the most magnificent deep-sky objects not to be included in the famous Messier catalog. Of course, Charles Messier (1730-1817) was looking for deep-sky objects that could be mistaken for comets. Maybe he thought nobody would see this pair of glittery clusters as a comet in the sky.

Although considered a deep-sky jewel, the Double Cluster is visible to the unaided eye in a dark country sky.

If you zoom in on them with binoculars or a wide view telescope, you’ll see them as two glorious star clusters. Also they’re an easy target through a telescope and will wow your friends!

The position of h Persei is Right Ascension: 2h 19m; Declination: 57o 9′ north

The position of chi Persei is Right Ascension: 2h 22.4m; Declination: 57o 7′ north

The Double Cluster from our EarthSky Community

Bottom line: On any autumn or winter evening, scan between Cassiopeia and Perseus for the magnificent Double Cluster in Perseus. The stars in these two clusters are young, hot supergiant suns that are many thousands of times more luminous than our sun.

item.title: Another satellite breakup raises concerns about space junk - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter.

Another satellite breakup raises concerns about space junk

This week, a Soviet-era weather satellite broke apart in low-Earth orbit, creating tens of new pieces of debris that could threaten other spacecraft. This information comes from LeoLabs, a company that operates a global network of radars for tracking satellites and space debris. LeoLabs said that it detected the event on October 5, 2026, with the company’s system, LeoLabs Delta. It spotted multiple objects near the inactive Meteor 2-7 satellite after it passed over a radar station in Western Australia. Follow-up observations from other radars confirmed that a debris-generating event occurred.

LeoLabs said the event is the latest in a series of debris-generating events its network has detected over the past six months. The company called it a:

… worrying trend for space safety and security.

A satellite launched in 1981

The satellite that broke up — Meteor 2-7 — was launched by the Soviet Union in May 1981. It was part of the Meteor series of weather satellites. Its purpose was to observe clouds and gather information about Earth’s atmosphere.

But the satellite has now been inactive for decades. Today, it travels around Earth at an altitude of roughly 500 to 560 miles (800 to 900 km), according to orbital data.

That altitude makes the new debris particularly concerning.

NASA says debris at about 500 miles (800 km) can remain in orbit for decades or even centuries, depending on its size and other factors. The atmosphere is simply too thin at that altitude to slow objects down quickly. The Meteor 2-7 debris could therefore remain a hazard to spacecraft for a very long time.

What happened to Meteor 2-7?

There are a couple scenarios that might explain why Meteor 2-7 broke up. First, an internal failure or explosion might have occurred. On the other hand, it might have collided with another object in low-Earth orbit.

Jim Shell, an orbital debris expert, has narrowed down the time of the event to 09:45 UTC +/- 10 minutes on October 5, 2026. Shell speculates the cause might have been a collision but said it will likely remain a mystery. Shell said on X:

Meteor 2-7’s altitude of 855 km is in a dense region for orbital debris. Might we have experienced an impact from one of the numerous untracked debris objects? It is furthermore observed that the event time estimate places the 81 degree inclined satellite near its highest latitude position where the debris spatial density is highest. We will likely never know….

A growing orbital debris problem

This isn’t the first recent fragmentation event to attract attention. In March, LeoLabs detected dozens of objects around the SpaceX Starlink 34343 satellite after it experienced an anomaly. SpaceX said the event was probably due to an internal energetic source rather than a collision. In August, LeoLabs also detected the fragmentation of a Chinese Long March rocket body, producing potentially tens to hundreds of fragments.

Each event adds more material to an already crowded orbital environment. Objects in low-Earth orbit travel at roughly 17,500 mph (28,000 km/h). At those speeds, even a small piece of debris can seriously damage or destroy a spacecraft. NASA estimates that there are hundreds of thousands of pieces of debris at least a centimeter across, along with millions of smaller fragments.

Could this lead to the Kessler Syndrome?

The growing number of objects raises the specter of Kessler Syndrome, a potential chain reaction in which collisions create debris, that debris causes more collisions, and those collisions create still more debris.

NASA scientist Donald Kessler and NASA colleague Burton Cour-Palais proposed the concept in 1978. The concern isn’t that one satellite breakup will suddenly create an impenetrable cloud around Earth. Instead, repeated collisions over many years could gradually make certain orbital regions increasingly hazardous. And each new satellite breakup brings us closer to an unstoppable chain of events.

Read more about the Kessler Syndrome

item.title: Did formaldehyde on ancient Mars help kickstart life? - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

  • We know that Mars once had lots of water on its surface. And a new study says there might have been formaldehyde in some of that water.
  • Atmospheric formaldehyde was likely brought down to the surface through rainfall, the researchers in Japan suggests.
  • In water, formaldehyde can kickstart the chemical reactions to produce the sugars and organic molecules needed for life.

Follow the ancient rains on Mars

Did life once exist on Mars? Various clues in recent years have moved the answer toward “quite likely.” But we still don’t know for sure. Now there’s another possible clue: formaldehyde.

Scientists said on October 1, 2026, that atmospheric formaldehyde could have mixed with rainwater billions of years ago. And in water, formaldehyde can help start chemical reactions that produce sugars, amino acids and other complex organic molecules needed to start life.

The researchers — from Tohoku University, the Earth-Life Science Institute and the Institute of Science Tokyo in Japan — wanted to know where this formaldehyde would have actually been present on Mars’ surface. The new study makes some interesting findings.

The intriguing new peer-reviewed results were published in The Planetary Science Journal on September 30, 2026.

Formaldehyde on ancient Mars

We know that Mars once had plentiful water on its surface, including rain, rivers, lakes and a probable ocean. And some studies have shown that the early atmosphere on Mars likely produced formaldehyde, a pungent, colorless gas.

Why is that important? When formaldehyde is mixed in water, something very interesting happens. Chemical reactions create sugars, amino acids and other complex organic molecules. These are the molecules needed to help give a kickstart to life.

Where was the formaldehyde?

If there was formaldehyde on Mars long ago, where exactly was it? The researchers created a global map showing where the gas would most likely have been located on the surface.

They simulated the warmer conditions of the time, about 3.8 to 3.6 billion years ago. With this model, the researchers studied how temperature, water vapor, pressure and ultraviolet (UV) light affected the formation of formaldehyde.

The results indicated that water vapor was of particular importance. First, UV light broke down the water molecules. This released reactive hydrogen , which was needed to form the formaldehyde.

Then, rains brought the formaldehyde down to the surface. Based on this, the researchers concluded that areas with more water had more formaldehyde. So basically, the water cycle determined which areas would have more formaldehyde.

Lead author Shungo Koyama at the Institute of Science Tokyo and Tohoku University said:

By comparing our map with findings from rovers, we can begin to test whether places that received more H2CO were also more favorable for early life-related chemistry. If future observations confirm this relationship, our map could help identify promising targets for future Mars missions.

Mountainous regions get the most formaldehyde

As it turned out, mountainous regions received the most rainfall and had the most formaldehyde. In fact, regions like Tharsis and Elysium had 10 times more formaldehyde than the global average. Both areas have huge towering volcanoes.

To note, this estimate is for how much formaldehyde Mars had way back then, not now.

Did formaldehyde help start life on Earth?

Back in 2011, another study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showed that formaldehyde might have also helped start life on Earth.

Scientists think that billions of years ago, a Mars-sized object slammed into the Earth, blasting out debris that formed the moon. The collision, most experts say, caused huge numbers of organic molecules to flee our planet. But sticky formaldehyde molecules held onto a fair chunk of Earth’s carbon that we might have otherwise lost. We might owe our existence to that ancient formaldehyde.

Bottom line: Formaldehyde in the ancient rains on Mars might have provided crucial chemical reactions needed for life to begin on the red planet billions of years ago.

Source: Global Distribution of Atmospheric Formaldehyde Deposition Correlated with Water Vapor on a Warm Early Mars

Via Tohoku University

Smile mission releases its 1st stunning aurora footage!

The Smile mission released its first aurora footage on September 30, 2026. And it’s stunning! The mission is a collaboration of the European Space Agency and the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Its goal is to understand how the solar wind interacts with Earth’s magnetosphere, or protective magnetic field.

In the image above, we see the auroral oval glowing in ultraviolet light around Earth’s North Pole. Smile is the first spacecraft since 2008 to capture this complete auroral ring in UV light. And it can watch Earth for a record 45 hours at a stretch. The video covers 00:00 to 00:58 UTC on July 24, 2026, while Smile was still being commissioned in space.

An X-ray challenge

The Smile mission also includes an X-ray camera. But during the testing phase, scientists saw that the X-ray camera was capturing too much stray light. So teams are working on updating settings to fix this issue. They hope that soon they will be able to take a good X-ray image of the magnetopause (where the solar wind meets Earth’s magnetic field). They would also like images of the northern polar cusp. This cusp is a hole near the North Pole where charged solar wind particles funnel toward Earth’s surface.

In total, Smile has four instruments with which to observe sun-Earth interactions. They are a magnetometer, a light ion analyzer, the ultraviolet imager and the soft X-ray imager. ESA says the ultimate goal of Smile is to:

… improve our understanding of solar storms, geomagnetic storms and the science of space weather.

Bottom line: The Smile mission has shared its first footage of Earth’s auroral oval, and it’s a stunner! Read more about the mission here.

item.title: Black holes could have planets, new simulations suggest - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• Could black holes have planets? New research says yes, they could.
  • New simulations suggest massive planets could form in the outer dusty regions around supermassive black holes.
  • The planets could form through a similar mechanism to how planets form around stars.

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

Supermassive black holes could have planets

Astronomers have found thousands of planets orbiting other stars. They’ve even found some rogue planets, or planets without a star. Now, fascinating new research says more planets could be lurking elsewhere. They could, the study says, be forming around black holes.

Astrophysicists Bhupendra Mishra and Wladimir Lyra discussed the possibility on a SETI livestream on September 21, 2026. They revealed that massive planets could form in the dusty regions around supermassive black holes, similarly to how planets form around stars.

The simulations suggest these planet-mass objects could start around the mass of Jupiter and then keep growing. And, incredibly, a single active black hole could spawn millions of planets at a time.

The new peer-reviewed paper was originally published in The Astrophysical Journal on June 29, 2026.

Watch a recording of the SETI Live livestream.

A birthplace for planets?

Scientists think supermassive black holes can be found in the central regions of almost all large galaxies. This study focuses on supermassive black holes that are actively feeding on the gas and dust around them. These incredibly violent objects are known as active galactic nuclei, or AGNs.

When these AGNs pull in matter to devour, the gas and dust start to collect and move around the black hole in a blazingly hot accretion disk. These are similar to the accretion disks that form around stars and create planets.

Noticing this, astrophysicist Barry McKernan — a co-author of the new study — asked Lyra whether the processes that form planets around stars could also occur around an active galactic nucleus.

They found that it could happen, at least theoretically. This is because the same physics should underly the process even in the different environments. If so, black holes could have planets.

The scales are vastly different though. A supermassive black hole could be a million times more massive than the sun. And baby planets forming around it could start out with the mass of Jupiter, our solar system’s biggest planet.

They would also form farther out from the black hole, in the dusty outer region of the disk. That is analogous to the outer region of our solar system, where comets form.

How would planets form?

So just how would one of these massive planets form? The researchers say the process would be similar to the way planets in regular solar systems do: from colliding dust. Dust grains would accumulate in increasingly dense concentrations. That’s the beginning of a baby planet.

Streaming instability — when drag on solid particles within a disk of gas and dust causes them to spontaneously clump — is the process behind this accumulation.

It’s even possible that some of them could grow beyond the planet stage and become brown dwarfs. These “failed stars” are larger than typical planets, but not massive enough to sustain nuclear fusion and shine like stars.

And, incredibly, some of those could keep growing until they became true stars.

How long would they last?

But some black hole planets might face a dire fate. Gravity from the black hole could move some of them inward. The temperatures in that region closer to the black would be far too hot. The planets would disintegrate. This, in turn, would create more dust.

That said, there could be a lot of planets to go round. The researchers estimated that a million planets could form during a single active episode of an active galactic nucleus. One of these bursts is typically about 2 million years long. And a black hole can go through many of these periods in its lifetime. Add that up over billions of years, and the number of planets formed from a black hole could be immense.

Can black hole planets be detected?

Right now, we can’t directly detect any of these planets, if they exist. That will require new methods. The black holes are too massive to use the radial velocity technique, which detects the slight movement of a star caused by an orbiting planet.

The transit method — when a planet passes in front of its star as seen from Earth — might work, but the planets, big as they are, would be vanishingly small compared to the accretion disk of dust around the black hole. And that would be the only background light source available, since the black hole itself doesn’t emit light.

Gravitational microlensing could also work. But you would need several planets around the same black hole to produce a strong enough lensing signal, along with a favorable alignment. In gravitational microlensing, the mass of the planet distorts the spacetime around it, which astronomers can detect.

It would also be difficult to discern a planet from all the other noise that is around a supermassive black hole.

Pretty much the last place in the universe I'd expect to find planets is in the incredibly violent and radiation-laden accretion disks around supermassive black holes.And yet… maybe? ? ?www.scientificamerican.com/article/plan…[thanks to @saavikford.bsky.social for a convo about this]? ?

— Phil Plait (@philplait.bsky.social) 2026-06-05T15:47:17.511Z

Is planet the best description?

Even though the underlying physics is similar, these planets still form in a very different environment than those that form around stars. So should we call them planets? The peer-review team for the paper actually objected to calling them planets. So Lyra suggested the term “blanets.”

But that term hasn’t come into use yet, so they are still just calling them planetary-mass objects.

Could black hole planets have moons?

If black holes can have planets orbiting them, then it’s natural to wonder if those objects could have moons. The researchers say that these worlds would be more likely to form as binaries. That is, two bodies of similar mass orbiting each other, rather than one body having a smaller body orbiting it as a moon. There are binary asteroids and minor planets like this in our solar system.

Angular momentum could cause this to happen. When the planets are first forming, angular momentum would produce binary systems in which two objects orbit one another. The same process occurs in the Kuiper Belt in our solar system. In fact, astronomers have discovered a growing number of binary objects there.

What about life?

Could any of these hypothetical planets support life? We don’t know, but it’s not impossible. The simulations suggest that they would have energy, even though black holes don’t emit light like a star. The energy would come from hot gas in the black hole’s accretion disk.

It’s fun to ponder what kind of light might be possible on such worlds. And what would it be like to stand on one of them and look at the glowing accretion disk swirling around the black hole.

Bottom line: New simulations by two astrophysicists suggest that supermassive black holes could have planets orbiting them, much like planets orbit stars.

Source: Active Galactic Nucleus Tori: Potential Birthplace to Millions of Planets

Via SETI Institute

item.title: Hera mission hits the brakes to arrive at asteroid - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
The Hera mission hits the brakes

ESA’s Hera mission is ready to hit the brakes! The spacecraft is headed for the site of a human-made impact on the asteroid Dimorphos, but first it has to slow down so it can properly reach it. Early Thursday, the spacecraft will fire its thrusters to slow it for its rendezvous with the asteroid Didymos and its tiny moon Dimorphos, which NASA hit with the DART spacecraft in 2022. The maneuver will be a tricky one. ESA said:

Hera will rotate around so that its ring of Orbit Control Thrusters face toward the Didymos system. Three of these hydrazine-based thrusters will be ignited at once, burning continuously for a total of 93 minutes, to reduce Hera’s velocity relative to the asteroids by a few hundred meters per second.

If all goes well, Hera should arrive at Dimorphos next month to begin its investigations!

Hera is ready for its asteroid rendezvous

In 2022, the groundbreaking DART mission struck and moved an asteroid. It was a test of Earth’s ability to defend itself from an incoming asteroid threat. Two years ago, on October 7, 2024, a follow-up mission – ESA’s Hera – launched toward the asteroid impact site on Dimorphos, a little moon of the asteroid Didymos. Now, Hera is almost ready for its November 2026 meeting with the asteroid pair. After it arrives, it will spend six months investigating the aftereffects from the impact.

So far in 2026, the Hera mission has undergone a deep-space maneuver to correct its course toward its target. And in July 2026, it finished receiving an upgrade to its software. This newest braking maneuver on October 15 should get the spacecraft to its target.

When Hera reaches the asteroids, it will release two cubesats, Milani and Junventas. Milani is in charge of spectral surface observations (splitting light bounced off the asteroid into a rainbow array of colors, then analyzing that light). And Juventas will take the first radar soundings in the heart of an asteroid.

When DART hit Didymos

Back in 2022, when DART hit Didymos’ little moon Dimorphos, it made a big splash. We know for sure it pushed the asteroid slightly out of its previous orbit. And the debris kicked up in the collision might even have created a new meteor shower for Earth!

Hera is going to learn more about just what happened when DART struck the little asteroid, creating a crater on its surface and moving it slightly in orbit. It’s going to learn more about Dimorphos itself, to help refine our knowledge of what DART did … to keep us safe from future asteroid collisions.

This will be the first investigation of a binary asteroid. Hera’s focus will be on Dimorphos, the moonlet that DART impacted. According to ESA – the mission planner – Hera will conduct a “crime scene investigation” at the little asteroid moon. But Hera will also check out both Didymos and the dusty environs unleashed by the impact.

Here are 3 mysteries that Hera will help solve

ESA shared 3 mysteries that Hera will help solve:

  1. Hera will measure the density and composition of Dimorphos in detail and help scientists determine whether it is a ‘rubble pile’ loosely held together by gravity, or a solid core covered in boulders and gravel.
  2. Hera will map the crater created by DART’s impact down to 4-inch (10-cm) resolution to help scientists better understand how the surface material responded to the collision. It’s possible that there is no crater at all, rather the impact reshaped the entire asteroid!
  3. About 15% of known asteroids are actually binary systems, but their origins remain mysterious. Hera will determine whether Dimorphos and Didymos are made from the same material, which would hint that the rapidly spinning Didymos once threw off debris into space that later formed Dimorphos.

Hera project scientist Michael Küppers

Watch EarthSky’s Deborah Byrd speak with Hera project scientist Michael Küppers below. Get the latest here about keeping Earth safe from asteroids.

The Hera mission and a missing planet

Watch a video about the Hera mission to the asteroids Didymos and Dimorphos.

The Hera mission vs the Colosseum

The asteroid Didymos is about a half mile (800 meters) wide. So, that’s about the size of the Golden Gate Bridge. Its little companion, Dimorphos, is about 560 feet (170 meters) in diameter. And that’s about the size of the Great Pyramid. Or compare it to Italy’s Colosseum below.

Bottom line: The Hera mission will hit the brakes this week as it slows down to reach Didymos and Dimorphos. These asteroids were the site of a human-made impact in 2022. Hera is going to investigate the aftermath.

Via ESA

item.title: The ghost of Biela’s Comet: It created 2 storms and disappeared - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
You deserve a daily dose of good news. For the latest in science and the night sky, subscribe to EarthSky’s free daily newsletter.

The ghost of Biela’s Comet

Have you ever heard of the Andromedid meteor shower? Nowadays, this late November meteor shower is so weak that it’s largely too dim to see with the unaided eye. But a couple of hundred years ago it surged in two spectacular meteor storms … before it largely disappeared. And, spookily, this shower comes from the ghost of a comet.

Biela’s Comet was a regular visitor to skies in the late 1700s and early 1800s. French astronomer Jacques Leibax Montaigne first recorded this comet in 1772. It wasn’t until 1826 that Austrian astronomer Wilhelm von Biela recognized that the comet came around every 6.6 years. So Biela’s predictions are what gave the comet its name.

But when Biela’s Comet returned in 1846, it put on a shocking show. At first the comet appeared distinctly pear shaped, according to The Facts on File Dictionary of Astronomy, and then it split in two some 10 days later. The two halves of Biela’s Comet continued traveling in practically the same orbit, with one about 174,000 miles (280,000 km) behind the other. The brightness of each comet half fluctuated wildly. The Dictionary of Astronomy then says:

At the next return in 1852, their separation had increased eightfold, the two periods different by about 15 days.

Neither comet has been seen since.

Meteor showers and meteor storms

While Biela’s Comet (or comets) may be gone, the meteor shower they spawned remains. The Andromedids (sometimes called the Bielids) is an annual meteor shower in late November. The radiant of the shower — the spot the meteors appear to radiate from — is in the constellation Andromeda the Chained Lady.

How do we know this meteor shower is related to the ghost of Biela’s Comet? The meteoroid stream — or the trail of pebbles left behind — has the same orbit as the comet had.

In fact, Biela’s Comet produced two meteor storms. Meteor storms are especially strong showers that produce at least 1,000 meteors per hour. And that’s what happened on November 27 of 1872 and again in 1885. The 1885 meteor storm was incredibly strong, with reports of 75,000 meteors an hour. However, the shower has been much quieter ever since. In general, the few meteors it produces today are so dim that they are not visible to the eye alone.

Bottom line: November’s Andromedid meteor shower is the product of the ghost of Biela’s Comet. This comet stunned observers in the 1800s when it broke up and then produced meteor storms.

item.title: Martian dawn pic from Curiosity rover highlights cliffs and crags - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

Martian dawn pic highlights cliffs and crags

NASA’s Curiosity rover has been exploring the Mount Sharp region of Mars since it arrived in 2012. Now, on October 6, 2026, NASA has released this new pic of a Martian dawn, which illuminates the play of light on the cliffs and crags of the region.

The Mars Curiosity rover captured this image back on August 11, 2026, which was the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol. And since then, Curiosity has surpassed the 5,000 sol mark and is still going strong!

An odd feature on Mars

NASA said the crags on the horizon are known as yardangs. These are landscape protrusions carved out of bedrock. The yardangs protrude on the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp.

Mount Sharp is a 3-mile-tall (5-km-tall) mountain, while the yardangs extend horizontally about 10 miles (16 km) across.

But scientists think something is odd about this yardang layer on Mars. Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said:

The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on. But that’s what makes it exciting to reach.

No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.

More about Mount Sharp

Mount Sharp lies within Gale Crater. And it makes up the crater’s central peak. Curiosity has now climbed 0.6 miles (1 km) of elevation as it ascends toward Mount Sharp. In fact, that’s the highest ever climbed on Mars, and the rover is still going.

Scientists say Mount Sharp is made of layers that formed over time. Lakes and streams once flowed here. But eventually, the water dried up and left behind salty deposits. The wind then eroded away some of the material, leaving behind the crags or yardangs.

Now the little Curiosity rover will roll onward, perhaps reaching the base of the yardangs by 2027. We look forward to seeing these jagged formations from a closer point of view!

Bottom line: On October 6, 2026, NASA released an image of Martian dawn from the Curiosity rover. The image captures a pale light illuminating distant cliffs and crags.
